meta.title: DNS Deep Dive — From Domain Names to Route 53 and Building Your Own DNS in Java
meta.author: Sandeep Tiwari
meta.summary: A deep practical tutorial on DNS covering domain names, DNS resolution, recursive and authoritative DNS servers, DNS record types, A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, SOA, PTR, SRV and CAA records, TTL and caching, Route 53, Alias records, Route 53 routing policies, DNS system design, reliability and security, and how to design and build a simplified DNS server in Java.

thumbnail.alt: DNS deep dive with Route 53 and Java DNS server architecture

content.tle: DNS Deep Dive — From Domain Names to Route 53 and Building Your Own DNS in Java
content.smr:
DNS looks simple when we say "domain name to IP address", but production DNS is a distributed system involving clients, caches, recursive resolvers, root servers, TLD servers, authoritative servers, delegation, TTL, routing policies and health checks.
This tutorial starts from the absolute basics and gradually builds the mental model required to understand DNS in AWS, Route 53, system design interviews and Java networking.
content.hd1: 1. DNS in Real Life — Why Do We Need It?
content.p:
Imagine you want to call your bank. You probably remember the bank's name rather than memorizing a telephone number for every service.
DNS provides a similar abstraction for computers. Humans use meaningful names such as api.example.com while computers ultimately communicate using network addresses such as IPv4 or IPv6 addresses.
Imagine an application running on an EC2 instance with the public IP 13.201.45.100.

list.item: Without DNS → users need to remember 13.201.45.100.
DNS resolves the name into information required to reach the service.

content.quote: DNS is the naming and resolution system that allows applications to use stable human-readable names instead of depending directly on network addresses.

img.alt: Real life analogy showing names mapped to addresses
img.caption: DNS maps human-friendly names to machine-oriented network information

content.p: Consider the hostname api.rotatingmind.com. It is easier to understand DNS if we break this name into components.

list.item: The final dot represents the DNS root.

content.p: The technically complete DNS name is api.rotatingmind.com. The final root dot is normally hidden from users.

img.alt: DNS domain name anatomy
img.caption: Breaking a DNS name into root, TLD, domain and hostname

content.p: DNS is not one giant database containing every domain on the Internet. It is a hierarchical and distributed system.

list.item: Top-Level Domain servers such as .com and .org.
Recursive resolvers that perform resolution on behalf of clients.

img.alt: DNS hierarchy from root to authoritative servers
img.caption: The hierarchical DNS architecture

content.p: The application or operating system that needs DNS information first contacts a configured DNS resolver.
A recursive resolver performs DNS lookups on behalf of the client. It can communicate with root, TLD and authoritative servers and cache the result.
Root DNS infrastructure helps the resolver discover the appropriate Top-Level Domain servers.
A TLD server knows which authoritative name servers are responsible for domains under that TLD.
An authoritative server stores the actual DNS records for a zone and provides authoritative answers.
content.hd1: 5. What Happens When You Type a URL?
content.p: Suppose a user enters https://api.example.com in a browser. Before the browser can establish the application connection, it normally needs to resolve the hostname.

list.item: The configured recursive DNS resolver receives the query.
The recursive resolver checks its cache.
If necessary, it queries the DNS hierarchy.
The root directs the resolver toward the appropriate TLD infrastructure.
The TLD infrastructure identifies the authoritative servers.
The authoritative server returns the DNS record.
The recursive resolver caches the result according to TTL.
The client receives the answer and can connect to the destination.

img.alt: Complete DNS resolution flow
img.caption: Complete recursive DNS resolution flow

content.quote: Important distinction: the client normally talks to a recursive resolver, while the recursive resolver performs the hierarchy traversal.
content.hd2: 5.1 The Recursive Resolution Algorithm — Formal Definition
content.p: "Recursive" here has a precise meaning that is easy to misread. From the client's point of view the resolver behaves recursively: the client asks one question and receives one final answer, with all intermediate work hidden. Internally, however, the recursive resolver almost always walks the hierarchy iteratively, hop by hop, and simply presents that work as a single recursive call to the client. Modeling this as a recursive algorithm is still the cleanest way to reason about it, because each hop is naturally expressed as "resolve the next, more specific server, then recurse into it."
The recursive resolver's job can be defined as a function resolve(name, type, server) that:

list.item: Checks its local cache for (name, type) and returns immediately on a cache hit.
Sends the query to the current server (root on the first call).
If the response is a final answer, caches it using its TTL and returns it.
If the response is a referral to a more specific server (e.g. root → TLD → authoritative), recursively calls resolve(name, type, referredServer).
If the response is a CNAME, recursively calls resolve(cnameTarget, type, root) to resolve the alias target.
Fails with NXDOMAIN or SERVFAIL when no further referral exists or a safety limit is hit.

content.p: Tracing resolve("api.example.com", A, root) against the ten steps introduced above produces the following recursive call chain. Each arrow is one recursive invocation, not a loop iteration.

list.item: resolve(api.example.com, A, ROOT) → root has no direct answer, but knows the .com TLD servers → referral.
resolve(api.example.com, A, TLD_COM) → TLD has no direct answer, but knows example.com's authoritative servers → referral.
resolve(api.example.com, A, AUTH_EXAMPLE_COM) → authoritative server holds the A record → final answer.
The final answer unwinds back through the recursive call stack, and each frame caches the record with its TTL before returning.

content.quote: Every "referral" response is exactly the trigger for the next recursive call: the base case is a final answer or an authoritative "no such record" response, and the recursive case is "ask a more specific server."

list.item: if depth greater than MAX_DEPTH: return SERVFAIL // guards against referral loops
if cached and not expired: return cached
if response is ANSWER: cache.put(name, type, response, response.ttl); return response
if response is CNAME: return resolve(response.target, type, ROOT, depth + 1)
if response is REFERRAL: return resolve(name, type, response.nextServer, depth + 1)

content.hd2: 5.4 Java Implementation of the Recursive Resolution Algorithm
content.p: The following Java sketch mirrors the pseudocode directly. It models DnsServerRef as "root, TLD, or authoritative server," and treats CNAME and referral handling as two distinct recursive branches, exactly like a classic tree/graph traversal.
A recursive algorithm is only safe if it is guaranteed to terminate. Three properties make resolve() well-behaved:

list.item: Progress toward a base case: every referral moves strictly toward a more specific zone (root → TLD → authoritative), so referrals cannot legitimately point backward.
Explicit base cases: an ANSWER or NXDOMAIN response always stops recursion, with no further recursive call issued.
A depth guard as a safety net: MAX_DEPTH (or an equivalent hop counter) converts a misconfigured or malicious referral loop into a fast SERVFAIL instead of unbounded recursion or a stack overflow.

content.p: In the worst case, without any caching, each recursive call corresponds to one network round trip and one additional stack frame, so resolving a name costs O(d) network calls and O(d) recursion depth, where d is the depth of DNS delegation for that name (typically 3 to 4: root, TLD, domain, and optionally a CNAME hop). With a warm cache, most calls short-circuit at the very first check in resolve(), making the amortized cost O(1) for previously seen names until their TTL expires.
content.hd1: 6. DNS Records — The Building Blocks of DNS
content.p: A DNS record describes information associated with a DNS name. A simplified record can be understood using four major concepts: name, type, value and TTL.

list.item: Name → Which DNS name does this record belong to?
Type → What kind of DNS information is this?
Value → What information should DNS return?
TTL → How long can the answer be cached?

content.p: api.example.com A 13.201.45.100 TTL 300 means that the IPv4 address associated with api.example.com can be cached for 300 seconds.
content.hd1: 7. A Record — DNS Name to IPv4 Address
content.p: The A record maps a DNS name to an IPv4 address.
Example:

list.item: The resulting IPv4 address can then be used for network communication.

img.alt: A record mapping domain name to IPv4
img.caption: A record: hostname to IPv4 address

content.hd1: 8. AAAA Record — DNS Name to IPv6 Address
content.p: AAAA records map a DNS name to an IPv6 address.
content.hd1: 9. CNAME — DNS Name to Another DNS Name
content.p: CNAME means Canonical Name. Unlike an A record, which directly provides an IPv4 address, a CNAME points one DNS name to another DNS name.
Example:

list.item: The client can ultimately obtain the address of the backend.

img.alt: CNAME DNS resolution
img.caption: CNAME creates an alias from one DNS name to another DNS name

content.quote: A record = name to IPv4. CNAME = name to another name.
content.p: Imagine your company changes its backend infrastructure from one provider to another. Instead of exposing infrastructure details to clients, application-facing DNS names can reference stable service names.
For example:
This creates a level of indirection between the application name and infrastructure endpoint.
content.hd1: 11. Why CNAME Has an Important Restriction
content.p: A traditional CNAME cannot normally coexist with other records at the same DNS name. This becomes important at the DNS zone apex.
The root of example.com already needs authoritative records such as NS and SOA. Therefore traditional DNS does not allow the zone apex to simply become a CNAME.
content.quote: DNS zone apex and CNAME behavior is one of the most important concepts to understand before learning AWS Route 53 Alias records.
content.p: MX records identify mail servers responsible for receiving email for a domain.
Example:
MX records contain priorities. Lower numerical values represent higher preference.
TXT records store text associated with a DNS name and are widely used for domain verification and email authentication mechanisms.
NS records identify the authoritative name servers for a DNS zone.

img.alt: DNS delegation using NS records
img.caption: NS records establish DNS delegation

content.p: The SOA record contains authoritative information about a DNS zone, including the primary authoritative server and operational parameters used by DNS infrastructure.
Normal DNS commonly maps names to addresses. Reverse DNS performs the opposite conceptual operation, mapping an IP address to a hostname.
SRV records can describe where a particular service is available, including target hostname and port information.
This makes SRV particularly interesting when connecting DNS concepts with service discovery and distributed systems.
CAA records can specify which Certificate Authorities are authorized to issue certificates for a domain.
This connects DNS with TLS certificate management and domain security.
content.hd1: 19. TTL — Why DNS Answers Are Cached
content.p: DNS would be extremely inefficient if every application request required a complete DNS hierarchy traversal. DNS therefore relies heavily on caching.
TTL defines how long a DNS answer can remain cached before it should be considered stale and refreshed.

img.alt: DNS resolver cache and TTL
img.caption: Recursive resolver caching DNS responses using TTL

list.item: High TTL → fewer DNS lookups and potentially longer propagation of changes.
Low TTL → changes can be observed sooner but may increase DNS query traffic.

content.p: DNS information can be cached at multiple layers.
content.quote: DNS changes are not always immediately visible everywhere because different caches can retain previous answers until their TTL expires.
content.p: Traditional DNS queries commonly use UDP port 53 because it has low overhead and is suitable for request-response DNS traffic.
TCP port 53 is also used in DNS for cases such as responses that require TCP transport and certain DNS server-to-server operations.

list.item: TCP → also required in specific DNS scenarios.

content.p: An attacker may attempt to provide false DNS information so that users are redirected to an unintended destination.
DNSSEC adds cryptographic mechanisms that allow DNS data authenticity and integrity to be validated.
content.hd2: DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS
content.p: Modern clients can protect communication between the DNS client and resolver using encrypted DNS transport mechanisms such as DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS.
Amazon Route 53 is AWS's managed DNS service. It provides DNS hosting, domain registration capabilities and DNS-based routing features.
A public hosted zone contains DNS information intended to be resolved through the public DNS system.
A private hosted zone provides DNS resolution inside associated AWS VPCs. It is useful for internal application names and service discovery.

img.alt: Route 53 public and private hosted zones
img.caption: Public and private Route 53 DNS

content.p: Route 53 Alias records provide AWS-specific DNS integration for supported AWS resources. They are especially important when pointing a DNS name to resources such as an Application Load Balancer or CloudFront distribution.
Example:

list.item: api.example.com → Route 53 Alias → Application Load Balancer.

content.quote: CNAME points to a DNS name. Route 53 Alias can point a DNS name to supported AWS resources.
content.hd1: 26. Real AWS Architecture — Route 53 + ALB + EC2
content.p: Consider a Spring Boot application running on multiple EC2 instances.

img.alt: Route 53 ALB EC2 architecture
img.caption: Production-style Route 53, ALB and EC2 architecture

list.item: Route 53 provides the DNS answer for the API endpoint.
The request reaches the Application Load Balancer.
The ALB evaluates listeners and routing rules.
The ALB selects a healthy backend target.
The Spring Boot application processes the request.

content.p: Suppose production receives 90 percent of DNS traffic and a new canary environment receives 10 percent.

img.alt: Route 53 weighted routing
img.caption: Weighted DNS routing for gradual traffic migration

content.p: A global application may have deployments in multiple AWS Regions. Route 53 latency-based routing can direct clients toward the configured Region expected to provide lower latency.
A primary endpoint can be associated with a health-check-based failover configuration and a secondary endpoint can be used when the primary is considered unhealthy.
content.hd1: 28. DNS vs Load Balancer — Do Not Confuse Them
content.p: DNS routing and application load balancing happen at different layers of the architecture.

list.item: Route 53 → resolves and routes DNS queries.
ALB → distributes HTTP or HTTPS application traffic.

img.alt: Difference between DNS routing and application load balancing
img.caption: DNS routing versus HTTP load balancing

content.hd1: 29. System Design — How Would You Build DNS?
content.p: Now move from using DNS to designing DNS. This is where DNS becomes a distributed-systems problem.
Suppose an interviewer asks: "Design a DNS service that can resolve millions of domain names."
Start by identifying the responsibilities of the system.
content.hd1: 30. High-Level Architecture of Our Own DNS

img.alt: High level design of a custom DNS service
img.caption: High-level architecture for a custom DNS platform

list.item: Load balancer or DNS-level distribution selects a resolver node.
If cache hit exists, response is returned immediately.
If cache miss occurs, resolver looks up the authoritative record store.
The record and TTL are returned.
The DNS response is returned to the client.

img.alt: Custom DNS request flow with cache
img.caption: DNS request path with cache hit and cache miss

content.p: A simplified DNS record model can be represented using:
Zone: example.com. Name: api.example.com. Type: A. Value: 10.10.1.20. TTL: 60 seconds.
DNS is extremely latency-sensitive. A cache can avoid repeatedly querying the authoritative data store.
A cache entry must contain both the DNS value and its expiration information.
content.quote: DNS caching converts repeated expensive lookups into fast memory lookups, but cached information can become stale.
content.p: DNS intentionally accepts a degree of eventual consistency because caching is fundamental to its scalability.
If a record changes from one IP address to another, existing cached responses may continue to be served until their TTL expires.

list.item: Short TTL → faster changes but more resolver traffic.
Long TTL → lower query load but slower visibility of changes.

content.p: DNS resolver nodes should ideally be stateless so that more nodes can be added horizontally.

img.alt: Horizontal scaling of DNS resolver nodes
img.caption: Horizontally scalable DNS resolver architecture

content.p: Shared authoritative state can live in a distributed database or replicated storage system.
content.quote: DNS is infrastructure. If DNS becomes unavailable, applications can appear unavailable even when the application servers themselves are healthy.
content.p: Java applications interact with DNS constantly, even when developers do not explicitly write DNS code.
Consider:
http://api.example.com/orders
Before the application establishes a network connection, the hostname must be resolved to an address.
content.hd1: 38. DNS Resolution in Java with InetAddress
content.p: Java provides java.net.InetAddress for hostname resolution.
Example:

list.item: Java asks the underlying networking stack to resolve the hostname.
The operating system and configured DNS infrastructure participate in resolution.

content.quote: Most Java developers consume DNS indirectly through standard networking APIs rather than implementing DNS resolution themselves.
content.hd1: 39. DNS Inside a Java HTTP Client
content.p: Consider a Spring Boot service calling another service:
https://payment.example.com/payments

list.item: Java HTTP client receives the hostname.

img.alt: DNS resolution inside a Java HTTP client
img.caption: DNS to TCP to TLS to HTTP in a Java application

content.p: DNS caching can occur below the application level, and Java runtimes can also cache hostname resolution results.
This becomes important in long-running Spring Boot services because infrastructure addresses may change while the JVM remains alive.
content.quote: In production Java systems, DNS caching behavior must be understood when applications communicate with dynamic infrastructure.
content.p: DNS can also participate in service discovery.
Instead of hardcoding:
an application can use:
payment-service.internal:8080
DNS provides an abstraction between the service identity and the underlying network location.
Kubernetes heavily relies on DNS for service discovery. Applications can communicate using service names instead of hardcoded pod IP addresses.

list.item: Applications can communicate using DNS names.

content.quote: DNS is one of the fundamental abstractions that allows distributed applications to use stable service identities while infrastructure changes.
content.hd1: 43. Building a Simplified DNS Server in Java
content.p: To understand DNS deeply, build a small authoritative DNS server rather than immediately trying to reproduce the entire Internet DNS hierarchy.
Our first version will support:
content.quote: Start with a simplified authoritative DNS server. Add recursion, caching, persistence and clustering only after the protocol fundamentals work.

img.alt: Java DNS server low level architecture
img.caption: Low-level design of a simplified Java DNS server

content.hd1: 45. Java Domain Model for DNS Records
content.p: A clean object-oriented design can represent different DNS record types using a common abstraction.
This allows the resolver to work with the common DNS record abstraction while each record type handles its own value representation.
content.hd1: 46. Receiving DNS Queries Using Java UDP
content.p: DNS queries can be transported using UDP. Java provides DatagramSocket and DatagramPacket for UDP networking.

list.item: Parse the DNS header and question.
Send the response packet back to the client.

content.p: A DNS message contains a header followed by sections such as question, answer, authority and additional records.

img.alt: DNS packet structure
img.caption: Simplified DNS message structure

content.p: The DNS header contains identifiers and flags that allow the client and server to understand the query and response.
This distinction is critical when designing DNS systems.
The client asks the resolver to obtain the final answer.
A DNS server can respond with the best information it currently has, such as a referral to another server.

img.alt: Recursive versus iterative DNS resolution
img.caption: Recursive and iterative DNS resolution

content.hd1: 50. Build an Authoritative DNS Server First
content.p: Our first production-learning milestone is an authoritative DNS server. It does not need to recursively query root and TLD servers.
If the server owns example.local, it can directly answer:
Once authoritative resolution works, add caching to understand performance and TTL semantics.

list.item: Perform authoritative lookup when cache misses.
Store the result with expiration time.

content.p: DNS is a high-QPS workload. A single-threaded implementation can become a bottleneck as request volume increases.

list.item: Non-blocking or asynchronous downstream operations where required.

content.p: A Java implementation can start with a fixed ExecutorService and later evolve toward NIO or a high-performance event-driven architecture.
A simple implementation can use ConcurrentHashMap. Production systems need explicit expiration, memory limits and eviction behavior.

list.item: LRU/LFU policy → useful when memory is bounded.

content.hd1: 54. Turning Our Java DNS into a Distributed System
content.p: A single Java DNS process is not enough for a production-scale service. The next step is replication and horizontal scaling.

img.alt: Distributed Java DNS architecture
img.caption: Distributed DNS service with multiple resolver nodes

content.p: DNS provides an excellent distributed-systems example of the trade-off between fast cached responses and immediate visibility of changes.
If multiple resolver nodes cache records independently, a record update may not become visible to every resolver simultaneously.
content.quote: DNS teaches an important distributed-systems principle: caching improves scalability and latency, but introduces staleness.
content.p: Use multiple resolver instances and independent failure domains.
Use replicated authoritative storage and local caching where appropriate.
Distribute DNS infrastructure across independent network paths and availability zones.
Respect TTL and design record-update mechanisms carefully.
content.quote: For DNS, latency and availability are critical because DNS often sits before the application request itself.

list.item: What scale of DNS queries must be supported?
Is the service authoritative, recursive or both?
Which DNS record types are required?
What happens when a resolver fails?
What happens when the record database fails?
How will the system be monitored?

content.hd1: 59. Putting Everything Together — Production AWS Architecture

img.alt: Production AWS DNS architecture with Route 53 CloudFront ALB and EC2
img.caption: DNS and application architecture in AWS

list.item: Private Route 53 zone → internal service discovery.

content.p: DNS becomes much easier when you inspect real records from your terminal.
Create a small AWS environment and connect DNS to a real application.

list.item: Register or use an existing domain.
Create an Alias record pointing to an ALB.
Deploy a simple application behind the ALB.
Change the DNS target and observe TTL behavior.

content.hd1: 62. DNS Interview Questions You Should Be Able to Answer

list.item: Why can't a traditional CNAME normally be used at the zone apex?
What is an Alias record in Route 53?
What is the difference between recursive and authoritative DNS?
How does DNS work with an ALB?
How would you design a highly available DNS service?
How would you build DNS in Java?
How would you handle millions of DNS queries per second?
How would you design DNS caching?
How would you handle DNS record updates?

content.p: DNS should no longer be thought of simply as "domain name to IP address." It is a distributed naming, delegation, caching and routing system.

list.item: Route 53 → managed AWS DNS and routing.
Java → consumes DNS through networking APIs and can implement DNS using UDP/TCP.

content.quote:
The architect's mental model is: Client → Recursive Resolver → DNS Hierarchy → Authoritative DNS → Cached Answer → Application Endpoint.
The system designer's mental model is: Protocol → Data Model → Cache → Concurrency → Replication → Failure Handling → Consistency → Observability.
content.p: DNS is one of the best examples of distributed-systems engineering. It combines naming, hierarchical delegation, caching, eventual consistency, replication, failure handling, routing and network protocols.

Once DNS is understood at this level, services such as AWS Route 53, Kubernetes service discovery, Java HTTP clients, load balancers, microservice architectures and cloud networking become much easier to reason about.
content.quote: Don't memorize DNS record types. Understand what problem each record solves, where the answer comes from, how it is cached, and what happens when the infrastructure fails.
